fixes.explanation: Moses doesn't steer the flock away. He decides to do the opposite and go closer. He says, “I must go over and see this marvelous sight.” (Exodus 3:3) Curiosity wins this round.

Holy is right. God says, “Take off your sandals, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.” (Exodus 3:5) Moses is out in the wilderness at the mountain of God, and God is calling to him from the bush. The ground gets called holy, and the sandals come off.
Not quite. The text says, “At this, Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.” (Exodus 3:6) So he does hide his face. The text even gives the reason: he was afraid to look at God.

Pharaoh is right. God says, “I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people the Israelites out of Egypt.” (Exodus 3:10) Pharaoh is the king of Egypt. A few verses ago Moses was minding Jethro's flock, and now he's got a king on his schedule.

Good guess, since the Nile does show up later in this passage (Exodus 4:9). But it's not the place God names here. He says, “…all of you will worship God on this mountain.” (Exodus 3:12) Mountain, friend, not riverbank.

Right. God says, “This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered in every generation.” (Exodus 3:15) Forever, friend, not just for Moses' day. Every generation is a long line of people, and God says that's how long the name stands.
True. God tells Moses, “The elders of Israel will listen to what you say…” (Exodus 3:18) God says it before Moses goes anywhere. Moses gets to carry that promise with him.
God says the opposite. He knows the king “…will not allow you to go unless a mighty hand compels him.” (Exodus 3:19) It takes a mighty hand to compel him. That's not a quick yes.

That's right. God says every woman will ask “…her neighbor and any woman staying in her house for silver and gold jewelry and clothing…” (Exodus 3:22) That's what God tells Moses will happen when they leave. He had just said they would not go away empty-handed. (Exodus 3:21)

A sling shows up in another story, when David takes his sling to face Goliath, the Philistine champion (1 Samuel 17:4, 40). That's a different hand on a different day. Here the LORD asks what's in Moses' hand, and Moses answers, “A staff.” (Exodus 4:2)
There's fire earlier on this mountain, but it's in a bush, not in Moses' hand. Fair guess, though. When the LORD asks what he's holding, Moses says, “A staff.” (Exodus 4:2) No torch needed.
No swinging here, friend. The text says Moses threw the staff down, “…and it became a snake, and he ran from it.” (Exodus 4:3) Running and striking are very different plans. Moses picks running.

True. Moses reaches out and grabs the snake, “…and it turned back into a staff in his hand.” (Exodus 4:4) The LORD had told him to grab it by the tail. I think that took some nerve after running from it.

That's right. Moses took his hand out of his cloak, “…and when he took it out, his hand was leprous, white as snow.” (Exodus 4:6) The LORD had just told him to put it inside. It's the second sign the LORD gives him.
No glowing hands here, friend. The text says his hand was “…leprous, white as snow.” (Exodus 4:6) White like snow, not bright like the sun. Shining isn't in the verse.
Right. The text says, “…it was restored, like the rest of his skin.” (Exodus 4:7) The LORD has Moses put the hand back inside the cloak first. Then it comes out whole again.
Water on dry ground might make mud in my kitchen, but not here. The LORD says it “…will become blood on the ground.” (Exodus 4:9) Not mud, friend. Blood.

That's it. The LORD says, “Now go! I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” (Exodus 4:12) Moses doesn't have to come up with the words alone. The LORD promises help and teaching.

That promise isn't in the text. The LORD says, “I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say.” (Exodus 4:12) What He promises is help and teaching. Finest speaker in Egypt isn't in the verse.
Moses doesn't ask for another sign. The text says he replies, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” (Exodus 4:13) He had already been shown signs by then. His request is about who goes.
Moses doesn't ask for more time. He says, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” (Exodus 4:13) He isn't asking to wait. He's asking for another person to go.
Caleb comes later, as one of the men Moses sends to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:6). The brother the LORD names here is Aaron. (Exodus 4:14) Right book, wrong name, friend.

Joshua also shows up later, as one of the men Moses sends to scout Canaan (Numbers 13:8, 16). The LORD names Moses' brother, Aaron the Levite. (Exodus 4:14) Joshua is a good name, just not the one in this verse.

True. The LORD says of Aaron, “When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.” (Exodus 4:14) The LORD also says Aaron is now on his way to meet Moses. Moses had just asked for someone else to go, and the LORD answers with a brother who will be glad to see him.

It's a warmer picture than that. The LORD says of Aaron, “When he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.” (Exodus 4:14) That's what the LORD says will happen when Aaron sees Moses. Gladness is what's coming.
